weeks.title: Love Comes from God
weeks.theme: We love because we were loved first; the starting point of love is not the other person but God.
group: Read 1 John 4:7–12. According to John, who is the source of love? How is that different from the way you used to think about love?
Who or what do you most often look to for the feeling of being loved? Does that expectation leave you more at rest, or more anxious?
In what moment this week did you receive God’s love? Next week, in what one area would you like to return to him first?
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, find a brother or sister of the same gender and spend five minutes sharing with each other: “What is the one sentence I most need God to remind me of this week?” Pray for each other for one minute. When you get home, send that one sentence to a friend, only that sentence, with no explanation.
weeks.weekend: Set aside a time this weekend to receive love: go to a quiet place (a park, a church, or a riverbank all work) and spend thirty minutes alone, without looking at your phone. First meditate on 1 John 4:19, then read aloud to God the three sentences you wrote this week about your longing, your fear, and what you entrusted to him. Afterward, invite a friend to a simple meal and listen closely to them. It is fine not to talk about your relationship status at all.

lessons.title: God Is Love
lessons.hear:
Xiaoxin is twenty-nine, and her friends are getting married one after another. The question she asks herself most often is, “Why does no one love me?” It is a very honest question, but it hides an assumption: love comes from other people, and if no one gives it to me, I am empty.

John offers a different starting point: “love is of God” (1 John 4:7), and “God is love” (1 John 4:8). Love is not a scarce resource held in someone’s hands; love has a source, and that source is God himself. He does not merely “have” love; he “is” love.

Seen this way, the first lesson of dating is not “How can I be loved?” but “Have I returned to the source?” It is like a spring: if you only guard other people’s cups, you will always worry that your cup is empty; if you go to the spring first, you will have the strength to share the water with others.

So in the first week of this course, we are in no hurry to talk about a partner. We return to this source first.
lessons.light: The order of relationships is God, self, others, things. Xiaoxin’s difficulty is not that she has no partner, but that she has placed the source of “being loved” in other people, so the order is reversed. Jesus is my example: his life first stood firm in the Father’s love, and only then did he go out to love people. The Bible is my standard: the source of love is God. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he pours God’s love into our hearts. From the human viewpoint to God’s viewpoint: love is not something to beg from people but something to receive from God.
think: According to 1 John 4:7–8, where does love come from? What is the relationship between God and love?
Whom do I often look to for the feeling of being loved? Does that expectation make me relaxed, or anxious?
How can I return to God first today and receive his love?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for being the source of love. I admit that I often beg people for the love that only you can give, and so I am disappointed and anxious. Holy Spirit, today let me first receive your love, so that I no longer rush to grab hold of someone, and no longer blame myself for being lonely. I give you the longing in my heart. Amen.
lessons.do: Find a quiet five minutes today and copy 1 John 4:8 into your notebook. Next to it write one sentence: God is love, and he loves me. Read it aloud once before bed tonight.
lessons.quick: Love is not begged from people; it is received from God.
text: Beloved, let’s love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.
He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love.

lessons.title: Love Within the Triune God
lessons.hear:
On the night he was arrested, Jesus prayed to the Father: “for you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24). Before there were any human beings, before there was any romance, there was already a love at the very depths of the universe: the Father loving the Son, the Son responding to the Father, and the Holy Spirit flowing between them.

What does this have to do with us? Jesus’ prayer that night was also for those who would later believe in him, that we too would see his glory and live in this love. In other words, we are not standing outside the door of love, waiting for someone to open it; we have been invited in.

Imagine a child who grew up in the love of his parents and later begins to date. Of course he will get nervous, too, but he will not take a single remark from the other person as a verdict on himself, because his roots are not there. By contrast, a person with no roots in love can feel as if the sky is falling because of one message left on read.

This does not mean denying loneliness. It means knowing that our worth was settled by love before we met anyone.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his sense of security came from the Father’s love, not from the praise of the crowds. The Bible is my standard: love existed before the foundation of the world, and our worth is not decided by other people’s ratings. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lets us truly experience this love in our hearts. Selflessness is not thinking little of yourself; it is no longer relying on other people’s responses to prove yourself.
think: According to John 17:24, before what time did the Father already love the Son? What does that remind you about where love comes from?
Whose response most often makes me doubt my worth?
The next time a message or a cold shoulder leaves me panicking, what truth can I say to myself?
lessons.speak: Father God, thank you for loving Jesus before the foundation of the world, and for inviting me into this love. Put this truth into my heart, so that I no longer rely on other people’s responses to decide whether I have worth. I rest my heart in your love. Amen.
lessons.do: Whenever a message, a read receipt, or someone’s coldness makes you panic today, pause for ten seconds and say to yourself: my worth is not in this message. Then say one sentence of thanks to God.
lessons.quick: Before anyone loved me, God already did.
text: Father, I desire that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am, that they may see my glory which you have given me, for you loved me before the foundation of the world.

lessons.title: We Were Made for Love
lessons.hear:
Genesis says: “God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them” (Gen 1:27). To be made in his image means that we are born bearing God’s likeness, and also born with a longing to connect with God and with others.

Wanting to be loved and wanting to love others is not weakness, nor is it something to be ashamed of as “wanting a relationship too much”; it is a design God placed within us. The problem is never having the longing; it is whom we hand the longing to for fulfillment.

Ming is a twenty-five-year-old office worker who often felt guilty, wondering, “Do I long for romance too much?” So he deliberately suppressed it, which only made him more restless. Later he learned to say to God, “Lord, you placed this longing in me, and I give it to you.” His heart grew lighter, and he no longer rushed to quench his thirst with just any relationship.

Longing does not need to be destroyed; it only needs to be brought to the right place.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he was fully God and fully human, with real emotions and clear boundaries. The Bible is my standard: people are made in God’s image, so the longing for love is allowed. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he leads us to bring our longing before God. A person living for self expects others to fill the longing; a person living selflessly gives the longing to God and lets God lead.
think: According to Gen 1:27, in whose image were people made?
Is my longing to be loved marked by shame, suppression, or honesty?
In one sentence, how can I hand this longing over to God?
lessons.speak: God, thank you for making me in your own image and for placing within me the longing to love and be loved. Cleanse me of my shame and impatience about this longing, so that I can honestly bring it before you, neither suppressing it nor grasping. I am willing to wait for your leading. Amen.
lessons.do: In your notebook write three sentences: I long for…; I am afraid of…; Lord, I give it to you. You do not need to show them to anyone.
lessons.quick: Longing is a design, not a shame; give it to God, not to anxiety.
text: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

lessons.title: God Loved Us First
lessons.hear:
“But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom 5:8). Notice one detail: he loved us not after we became better, but while we were still sinners.

The most common fear in dating is this: “If the other person sees the real me, will they still love me?” So we package ourselves, please people, and hide. But the cross tells us that God has already seen us at our most real and most unpresentable, and he still chose us.

Xiaorong went through a painful breakup, and afterward always felt she was “not worthy.” She stayed a long time before this verse before she understood: her worth is not determined by how that relationship ended, but by the cross.

Only someone steadied by this love has the courage to be honest, and the strength to let go when it is needed.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he loved people when they did not deserve it. The Bible is my standard: God’s love is grace, not a reward. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he pours this love into our hearts so that we no longer rely on performance to earn love. A person living for self trades performance for being loved; a person living selflessly first receives being loved, then goes on to love others, and in the end gives the glory to God.
think: According to Rom 5:8, when did God show his love toward us?
Which part of myself do I fear being seen by others?
What is one thing I can honestly say today in front of a safe person?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for dying for me while I was still a sinner. Heal my thought that I must first become better in order to deserve love, so that I no longer package myself or please people, but can be honest in your love and rest in your love. Amen.
lessons.do: Do one small thing today that is “not for being liked”: no photo editing, no showing off. Honestly say one true feeling to God or to a trusted friend.
lessons.quick: At our most undeserving, God already loved us; there is no need to trade performance for love.
text: But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

lessons.title: Loved First, Then Able to Love
lessons.hear:
Looking back over this week, we have walked a path: the source of love is God, love existed before the foundation of the world, we were made for love, and God loved us when we least deserved it.

John sums it up in two sentences: “not that we loved God, but that he loved us” (1 John 4:10), and “if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another” (1 John 4:11). The order is clear: first be loved, and only then love.

This is the foundation of the whole course. Some people think you must first find the right person in order to be loved; others think you must first make yourself better to deserve loving someone. But the Bible’s order is: first receive, then share.

If this week you find that you are still anxious and still comparing, that does not mean you have failed; it means you have seen something that needs adjusting. Seeing is the beginning of change.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, living in the Father’s love; the Bible is my standard, for love comes from God; the Holy Spirit is my guide, letting us experience being loved. The order of relationships: first with God, then with myself, then with others. To let Jesus be King is to let his love be the starting point of all my feelings.
think: This week, which sentence gave me the most relief?
Where do I still place my hope of “being loved” in other people?
Where would I like to start making adjustments next week?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for showing me the source of love this week. Keep adjusting me, so that I first receive your love and then love others. Holy Spirit, remind me that every time I feel anxious, I should come back to you first. All the glory be to you. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal write two sentences: my biggest discovery this week; the one thing I will adjust. Then send a message of thanks to a friend who has walked with you.
lessons.quick: First receive, then share; this is the order of love.
text: In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another.

weeks.keyText: We love him, because he first loved us.

weeks.title: It Is Not Good for the Man to Be Alone
weeks.theme: Romantic love is God’s design, not a human invention; singleness and longing are both within his care.
group: Read Gen 2:18–20. Why did God say it is “not good for the man to be alone”? What does this remind you of?
Has anyone ever asked you, “When are you going to date (get married)?” What did you feel inside?
This week, which friend or brother or sister could you reach out to and tell about your loneliness or your need?
weeks.sunday: At the Sunday gathering, find a brother or sister you don’t usually talk to, greet him or her first, and ask: “Is there anything this week you need someone to pray for?” After listening, pray for that person for one minute. This is not about meeting a potential partner; it is about making the church a family that supports one another.
weeks.weekend: Plan a get-together this weekend that is “not for the sake of dating”: invite two or three friends to share a meal, take a walk, or play ball. Agree on one rule beforehand: no talking about relationship status; focus on asking about each other’s life and burdens this season. When you get home, write in your journal: Who made me feel accompanied? How can I accompany others?

lessons.title: The Designer’s Intention
lessons.hear:
Jie is thirty-two, and every time he goes back to church, someone pats him on the shoulder: “When are you going to invite us to your wedding banquet?” He answers with a smile, but his heart feels heavy for the rest of the day. He wonders whether he really is “missing something.”

Genesis has a remarkable detail here. On each day of creation, God said “good”; only once did God say “not good”: “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him” (Gen 2:18). This is the first “not good” in the Bible.

This sentence is about human design: people are not islands; we were made to walk with others and support one another. It does not declare that “unmarried people are lacking,” and it certainly does not urge everyone to hurry up and find a partner. What the Designer is saying is that people need relationships, and that God himself provides.

So there is no shame in longing for someone to walk with. What matters is whom we hand that longing to.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he was single, yet not lonely; his life was full of fellowship with people. The Bible is my standard: God said “not good for the man to be alone,” which shows that people need relationships; but no verse says that single people are less complete. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he keeps us company in loneliness and leads us toward trustworthy companions. From people’s pressure back to God’s design.
think: In Gen 2:18, why did God say it is “not good for the man to be alone”? Is this about human design, or about some people being lacking?
When others show concern about my relationship status, what is my most common reaction inside?
How can I honestly tell God about my feeling of loneliness today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for saying that I was not made to be alone. Heal the places where I have been hurt by other people’s questions, and heal my own comparing and self-blame about my relationship status. I am willing to hand my longing to you, and willing to let you lead me to trustworthy companions. Amen.
lessons.do: Say one honest sentence to God today: Lord, sometimes I feel lonely. Then send a message to a friend you trust, saying only: If you’re free this week, would you like to have a meal together?
lessons.quick: When God said “not good for the man to be alone,” he was speaking of human design, not saying that singleness is a defect.
text: The LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”

lessons.title: A Helper Comparable to Him
lessons.hear:
After God said “not good,” the next scene is intriguing. God brought all kinds of animals to Adam to name. He looked over all the livestock, the birds, and the wild animals, yet the text says: “for man there was not found a helper comparable to him” (Gen 2:20).

There are two reminders here. First, it is not just any “other person” who will do. The text speaks of “a helper comparable to him,” someone who truly matches him and can really walk with him. Second, Adam was not anxiously searching everywhere; while he was fulfilling his responsibility, caring for and governing the created world, God saw his need and provided for it himself.

This is not a formula: do your job well and a partner will come. But it reminds us that God knows our needs, and his provision is more accurate than our anxiety. When a person puts his energy into fulfilling his responsibilities and loving God and others, he does not need to keep asking himself every moment, “Who is the right person?”
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he focused on completing what the Father entrusted to him and was not hurried by people’s gaze. The Bible is my standard: God knows our needs and sees our loneliness. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he leads us to discern what kind of person can truly walk with us. A person living for self rushes to fill the gap; a person living selflessly first focuses on fulfilling responsibilities, then waits for God’s provision.
think: What does Gen 2:20 say Adam did not find? What does that remind you about “finding the right person”?
Am I now fulfilling my responsibilities and loving God and others, or spending all day focused on “finding a partner”?
In which responsibility can I be a little more wholehearted today?
lessons.speak: God, thank you for knowing my needs. Cleanse the anxiety in my heart, so that I do not grab hold of just anyone because I am lonely. Lead me to focus on doing well what you have given me to do, and let me still trust you while I wait. Amen.
lessons.do: Pick one responsibility you have been putting off today (work, family, service, or study), focus on it for thirty minutes, and when you finish, say one sentence of thanks to God.
lessons.quick: God’s provision is more accurate than our anxiety; fulfill your responsibilities first, then wait for him.
text: The man gave names to all livestock, and to the birds of the sky, and to every animal of the field; but for man there was not found a helper comparable to him.

lessons.title: Two Are Better Than One
lessons.hear:
Ecclesiastes says: “Two are better than one” (Eccl 4:9), and the reason is very practical: “if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow” (Eccl 4:10).

Notice that the word used here is “fellow,” not only “boyfriend and girlfriend” or “husband and wife.” The “two” the Bible speaks of is any kind of real companionship: friends, brothers and sisters, spiritual companions, and also a future spouse. This reminds us that a person’s greatest danger is not having no partner, but having no one to lift you up when you fall.

Xiaoqi is thirty and single. She has a regular prayer partner, and they meet twice a month to honestly share their recent weaknesses. Later, during an ambiguous relationship, she almost lost her way, and it was one sentence from her partner that pulled her back. She said: I may not have a partner, but I have someone who lifts me up.

Rather than only hoping for a partner, let us first become people who support one another.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he sent out his disciples two by two, and in Gethsemane he asked them to keep watch with him. The Bible is my standard: two people supporting each other is God’s design. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he prepares us to become trustworthy companions. A person living selflessly is willing to let weakness be seen, and willing to lift up others.
think: According to Eccl 4:10, what does a companion do when you fall?
Do I now have a companion with whom I can honestly share my weaknesses?
How can I become a companion to someone else?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for not leaving me alone. Give me trustworthy, godly companions, and let me be a dependable companion to others. Heal the pride that is afraid of letting my weakness be seen, so that I am willing to walk with others in the light. Amen.
lessons.do: Within the next two days, invite a trusted friend of the same gender and say frankly: I would like to ask you to be my prayer partner and to meet with me once a month.
lessons.quick: First become companions who support one another; then talk about the rest.
text: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.

lessons.title: Jesus’ Singleness and Family
lessons.hear:
Jesus lived thirty-three years without marrying and without a home of his own. Yet his whole life was lived in relationships: he had close disciples, he had the home of Martha, Mary, and Lazarus, and he ate and drank with people in the crowds.

The most moving moment is on the cross. In his most painful hour, his eyes still saw his mother and the disciple he loved standing nearby. He said to his mother, “Behold, your son!” and to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home (John 19:26–27). Just before dying, he built a new family for the people around him.

This is a great comfort to single people: singleness does not mean loneliness, and it does not mean having no family. Jesus lived out complete love in singleness, because his life stood firm in the Father’s love and he was willing to give that love to those around him.

Our calling is the same: whether or not we have a partner, we can become family to others.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he was single, yet lived out complete love, and even in pain he still cared for people. The Bible is my standard: God’s family is not only blood and marriage, but also our family in Christ. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he places us in the large family of the church, to love one another. A person living selflessly does not ask “Who will love me?” but “Whom can I love?”
think: On the cross, how did Jesus handle his last relationships?
In my life right now, whose “family” can I take the initiative to become?
What small thing can I do today to help a lonely person feel accepted?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for living out complete love in singleness. Keep me from thinking only about what I lack, and help me see who around me needs my love. Holy Spirit, place me in your family, so that I become family to others. Amen.
lessons.do: Today reach out to someone who looks lonely (a new friend, an older person, a neighbor who lives alone, or a newcomer at church), and spend three minutes greeting them by message or phone call.
lessons.quick: Singleness does not mean loneliness; love lets us become family to others.
text: Therefore when Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”
Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.

lessons.title: God’s Family
lessons.hear:
Jesus’ mother and brothers came looking for him, and people outside passed the message in. Jesus looked at those sitting around him and said: “whoever does the will of God is my brother, my sister, and mother” (Mark 3:35).

This is not a denial of blood ties, but a widening of the family’s circle: in Christ, we are one family.

Looking back over this week, we saw four things: romantic love is God’s design (Gen 2:18); God’s provision is more accurate than our anxiety (Gen 2:20); we need companions who support one another (Eccl 4:9–10); and the single Jesus still lived in relationships (John 19:26–27).

If this week you find that you still often keep “Does anyone love me?” in the back of your mind, there is no need to blame yourself. You can ask: In this family of the church, am I known? Do I know others? Sometimes we think what we lack is a partner, when what we lack is real companionship.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, living out love in relationships; the Bible is my standard, for God said it is not good to be alone, and also said that whoever does his will is his family; the Holy Spirit is my guide, bringing us into this family. The order of relationships: first with God, then with myself, then with others. To let Jesus be King is to let his family become my place of belonging.
think: This week, which sentence comforted me most?
In this family of the church, are there one or two people who truly know me?
What will I take the initiative to do next week to become family to someone else?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for making me a member of your family. Correct my attitude of only hoping to be loved while being unwilling to enter other people’s lives. Holy Spirit, lead me to truly know people in the church, and to be known. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal write: my biggest discovery this week; who is the brother or sister I trust most at church; whom I will pray for this week. Then tell that person the name you wrote, and say: This week I am praying for you.
lessons.quick: Those who do God’s will are all his family; let us walk together.
text: Looking around at those who sat around him, he said, “Behold, my mother and my brothers!
For whoever does the will of God is my brother, my sister, and mother.”

weeks.keyText: The LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”

weeks.title: Singleness Is an Honorable Calling
weeks.theme: Singleness is not a defect, nor a waiting room for marriage, but a season God can use.
group: Read 1 Cor 7:7. How does Paul view singleness and marriage? How is that different from what you thought before?
Is your singleness right now more like waiting, choosing, or being forced? Which part do you most need God to comfort?
In this season, what concrete thing can you do to devote yourself to serving the Lord or loving others? Ask your group to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, ask yourself one question: In this season, what time and energy do I have that married people find hard to have? Then find a way to serve at church and use your freedom to love people: give an older person a ride, keep a newcomer company, or join a short-term mission trip.
weeks.weekend: Plan a half day of “focus” this weekend: turn off your notifications and do three things: one hour of devotions and prayer, one hour of serving or visiting someone, and one hour of doing something you love (exercise, reading, or creating). Afterward, write down: In this season, what is the freedom God has given me?

lessons.title: Each Has His Own Gift
lessons.hear:
Xiaomei is thirty-one and single, and very active in church. But every time she hears someone say, “He just hasn’t met the right person yet,” she feels as if something about her is “not good enough.”

Paul said something different: “each man has his own gift from God, one of this kind, and another of that kind” (1 Cor 7:7). The “gift” he speaks of is given by God. Marriage is a gift, and singleness is a gift. Neither is a reward, and neither is a punishment.

He does not say that singleness is more spiritual, nor that marriage is more mature. He certainly does not say that everyone is called to be single for life. He only says that each person’s path is different, and so is the gift God sets apart for each.

So rather than asking, “Why am I still single?” ask: “What has God entrusted to me in this season?”
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: in singleness he lived out complete love and mission. The Bible is my standard: both marriage and singleness are gifts from God, and neither is higher than the other. The Holy Spirit is my guide: in every season he leads us to live in a way that pleases God. A person living for self measures himself by whether he has a partner; a person living selflessly asks, “What does God want me to do in this season?”
think: According to 1 Cor 7:7, where do marriage and singleness come from?
Do I often measure my worth by whether I have a partner?
In this season, what has God entrusted to me?
lessons.speak: God, thank you for saying that singleness is not my flaw. Remove the voice in my heart that says “not good enough,” and do not let me compare myself with other people’s situations. Let me see what you have entrusted to me in this season. Amen.
lessons.do: Write down three sentences today: In this season, the freedom I have is…; I can use it to love…; what I want to thank God for is….
lessons.quick: Singleness and marriage are both gifts from God, and neither is higher than the other.
text: Yet I wish that all men were like me. However, each man has his own gift from God, one of this kind, and another of that kind.

lessons.title: Devoted to the Lord
lessons.hear:
Paul goes on to say something very practical: “He who is unmarried is concerned for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord” (1 Cor 7:32). He is not saying that married people are inferior. He is simply pointing out honestly that a person with a spouse must divide his attention between his spouse and his family, while a single person has a different kind of freedom in time and energy.

Then he says that he is speaking for their benefit, not to restrict them, but so that they may do what is appropriate and serve the Lord without distraction (1 Cor 7:35). His intention is not to limit people but to help them live well.

Xiaoyu is thirty and single, and he noticed that he has several more free evenings each week than his friends. He began regularly leading a college Bible study and meeting regularly with a teenager. He said: I used to think these open hours were “gaps because I have no partner,” but now I know they are space God has given me for service.

Freedom is not meant to be whiled away; it is meant to be spent on love.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his whole life was devoted to completing the Father’s will, without distraction. The Bible is my standard: a single person can have the freedom to devote himself to serving the Lord, and a married person can serve the Lord too, only in a different way. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he points out where I can invest myself in this season. A person living selflessly offers his freedom to God rather than spending it on filling up loneliness.
think: According to 1 Cor 7:32, where is the focus of an unmarried person’s concern?
What do I mostly use my free time for now?
What block of time can I devote to serving the Lord or loving others?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for giving me the freedom of this season. Do not let me use it only to pass the time in loneliness, but to know you, love others, and serve you. Holy Spirit, lead me to find the place where you want me to invest, and give me lasting strength. Amen.
lessons.do: Choose a regular time slot (once a week, at least two hours) set aside for serving people or being alone with God, and put it on your calendar right now.
lessons.quick: Freedom is not meant to be whiled away; it is meant to be spent on love.
text: But I desire to have you to be free from cares. He who is unmarried is concerned for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord;
but he who is married is concerned about the things of the world, how he may please his wife.

There is also a difference between a wife and a virgin. The unmarried woman cares about the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit. But she who is married cares about the things of the world—how she may please her husband.
This I say for your own benefit, not that I may ensnare you, but for that which is appropriate, and that you may attend to the Lord without distraction.

lessons.title: For the Sake of the Kingdom
lessons.hear:
When Jesus spoke about marriage and divorce, the disciples said it would be better not to marry. Jesus answered: “Not all men can receive this saying, but those to whom it is given” (Matt 19:11), and then: “He who is able to receive it, let him receive it” (Matt 19:12).

These two sentences carry two reminders. First, not everyone has the calling to singleness. Jesus did not require everyone to stay unmarried, and he did not say that singleness is a higher road. Second, if someone chooses singleness for the sake of the Kingdom, that is a reception given by God, not something that comes out of frustration or spite.

So there is no need to force yourself: “I must be single,” and no need to force yourself: “I must hurry up and get married.” You can honestly say to God: “Lord, right now I don’t know my calling. I am willing to be faithful in this season and wait for you to speak.”

Being honest before God is more powerful than rushing to draw a conclusion for yourself.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he respects each person’s path and does not force anyone. The Bible is my standard: singleness is a reception given by God, neither compulsion nor a ranking. The Holy Spirit is my guide: at the proper time he makes our path clear. A person living selflessly does not draw conclusions for God, but is honest and obedient before him.
think: According to Matt 19:11, can everyone receive this saying?
Do I often rush to draw a conclusion about my situation?
How can I honestly say “I don’t know yet” before God?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for respecting my path. I am not yet sure of your calling for me; do not let me decide out of impatience or spite. I am willing to be honest before you, and willing to wait for your clear leading. Give me your peace. Amen.
lessons.do: Spend five minutes today telling God: Lord, I don’t know what my calling is; I am willing to be faithful in this season. Then write this prayer in your journal.
lessons.quick: There is no need to draw conclusions for God; honestly saying “I don’t know yet” is also faith.
text: But he said to them, “Not all men can receive this saying, but those to whom it is given.

For there are eunuchs who were born that way from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the Kingdom of Heaven’s sake. He who is able to receive it, let him receive it.”

lessons.title: Faith in Waiting
lessons.hear:
“Wait for the LORD. Be strong, and let your heart take courage. Yes, wait for the LORD” (Ps 27:14). David says “wait” twice, with a line in between: be strong, and let your heart take courage.

This shows that waiting is neither passive daydreaming nor resentful endurance. Waiting takes courage: choosing to trust God while others get married one after another, while family members ask you questions, and through lonely nights.

Afang is thirty-three, and she set three habits for herself: reading the Bible for ten minutes every morning, meeting with a companion once a week, and doing one thing each month that helps her grow (learning a new skill). She said: Waiting is not doing nothing; it is living life well and keeping your mind on God.

Taking courage does not mean having no feelings; it means choosing to trust even when you have them.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: in the agony of Gethsemane, he still chose to obey the Father. The Bible is my standard: waiting is faith with courage. The Holy Spirit is my guide: in loneliness he comforts us and strengthens our hearts. A person living selflessly neither grasps nor gives up while waiting, but places his hand in God’s hand.
think: How many times does Ps 27:14 say “wait”? What encouragement is placed in between?
When I wait, which feeling most often shows up (restlessness, self-pity, numbness, fear)?
What small habit can I set for myself to make the days of waiting stronger?
lessons.speak: LORD, I will wait for you. Strengthen my heart, so that I do not lose courage when I am lonely, questioned, or compared. Lead me to live this season with your presence, with growth, and full of hope. Amen.
lessons.do: Set one small habit for this month and write it down: a daily time of devotions, a weekly time with a companion, or learning something new once a month. Do the first one today.
lessons.quick: Waiting is not daydreaming; it is faith with courage.
text: Wait for the LORD. Be strong, and let your heart take courage. Yes, wait for the LORD.

lessons.title: Satisfied in the Lord
lessons.hear:
Looking back over this week, we have seen that singleness is a gift from God (1 Cor 7:7); freedom can be used to serve wholeheartedly (1 Cor 7:32–35); God’s calling is not the same for everyone (Matt 19:11–12); and waiting takes courage (Ps 27:14).

Finally, we return to the psalmist’s prayer: “God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Ps 73:26). Asaph saw the wicked prospering while he himself suffered, and his heart nearly slipped. Later he entered God’s sanctuary and understood: apart from God, in heaven or on earth, there is nothing that can truly satisfy him.

This does not mean we do not need people’s love. It means that people’s love is a gift from God, not the foundation of our lives. The foundation is God himself.

When a person finds satisfaction in God, he enters relationships in order to give, not to fill a hole.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, satisfied in the Father; the Bible is my standard, for both singleness and marriage are gifts; the Holy Spirit is my guide, leading me in every season. The order of relationships: first with God, then with myself, then with others. To let Jesus be King is to let him be my portion, and all the glory goes to God.
think: This week, which truth comforted me most?
In Ps 73:25–26, what does the psalmist count as his portion?
Which “gap” do I most want to hand over to God to fill right now?
lessons.speak: God, besides you I desire nothing in heaven or on earth. Be my strength and my portion. Correct my thought that treats people as the foundation, so that I am satisfied in you and also have the power to love others. All the glory be to you. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal write: my biggest discovery this week; what I have been trying to use to fill the emptiness in my heart; I decide to give it to God. Then pray for a single or lonely friend.
lessons.quick: A person satisfied in God enters relationships to give, not to fill a hole.
text: Whom do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you.
My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.

weeks.keyText: Yet I wish that all men were like me. However, each man has his own gift from God, one of this kind, and another of that kind.

weeks.title: God’s Timing and Will
weeks.theme: Waiting is not a waste; God’s timing is more accurate than our anxiety.
group: Read Prov 3:5–6. In a relationship, what might it look like to “lean on your own understanding”?
In what relationship matter have you most wanted to “hurry up” lately? What are you afraid of?
This week, what is one thing you are willing to specifically entrust to God? Ask your group to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, find an older person whose life, whether married or single, has been steady, and ask: “In your days of waiting, how did God lead you?” Listen carefully without rushing to argue, and when you get home, write down one sentence they said.
weeks.weekend: Plan a “slow down” activity this weekend: walk for one hour without earbuds. As you walk, tell God the one thing you are most anxious about, then entrust it to him. When you get home, write in your journal: What I am willing to let go of is…; what I am willing to wait for is….

lessons.title: Trust in the LORD
lessons.hear:
After Xiaojie broke up with his girlfriend, he met another girl within three months. When friends asked whether it was too fast, he said, “I’m afraid that if I slow down, there will be no one left.”

Many people share this fear. Proverbs gives clear guidance: “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding” (Prov 3:5), and then: “he will make your paths straight” (Prov 3:6).

Intelligence is not a bad thing, but relationships are where it most easily fails: we use criteria, plans, and timetables to make decisions for ourselves, and forget to ask God. Proverbs says to acknowledge him in all our ways, not only to remember him when trouble comes.

“With all your heart” means putting your whole self on him. God is not our backup plan after our plans fail; he is the starting point of every step we take.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: in everything he first sought the Father’s will, and even before choosing his disciples he prayed all night. The Bible is my standard: do not lean on your own understanding; acknowledge God in all things. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he directs each of our steps. A person living for self hurries to arrange things himself; a person living selflessly first seeks God, then steps forward.
think: According to Prov 3:5–6, what must we not lean on? Whom are we to trust with all our heart?
In relationships, which kind of understanding do I most often lean on (plans, criteria, timetables, intuition)?
In what matter can I ask God first today, and decide afterward?
lessons.speak: LORD, I will trust in you with all my heart. Forgive me for so often leaning on my own understanding and hurrying to arrange things myself. Direct my path in every decision, and let me come before you first before I take the next step. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, on one relationship or interpersonal decision you are facing, stop first and pray for three minutes: Lord, I give this to you; please guide me. Then write the prayer in your journal.
lessons.quick: God is not our backup plan after our plans fail, but the starting point of every step.
text: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding.
In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.

lessons.title: Beautiful in Its Time
lessons.hear:
“He has made everything beautiful in its time” (Eccl 3:11). The sentence is short, but powerful. It says that beauty comes not from being fast but from being timely.

Seeds sprout in spring, fruit ripens in summer, and each thing shows its beauty only at the right time. Relationships are the same: too early may hurt someone; too late is nothing to panic about.

Ecclesiastes goes on to say that God has also set eternity in their hearts, yet man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end (Eccl 3:11). This is a humbling reminder: we cannot fully see through God’s timing. We often think, “I know when is best,” but really we see only a small part.

So waiting is not proof that we have been forgotten; it is where we learn to hand our time to the One who sees farther than we do.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he said his time had not yet come, and he went to the cross only at the time God had set. The Bible is my standard: God makes everything beautiful in its time. The Holy Spirit is my guide: when the time is full, he leads us forward. A person living for self wants to control time; a person living selflessly hands time to God.
think: According to Eccl 3:11, what does God make of everything in its time?
Which “timing” is hardest for me to accept right now?
How can I hand my time over to God in this matter?
lessons.speak: God, I admit that I often want to control time, and that I often get anxious over other people’s progress. Teach me to believe that you make everything beautiful in its time. Let me learn obedience while I wait, and learn to enjoy today’s grace. Amen.
lessons.do: Write one sentence in your journal: I am willing to hand my “time” over to God. Then choose one small thing you can truly enjoy today (a meal, a walk, a phone call) and experience it with full attention.
lessons.quick: Beauty comes not from being fast but from being timely.
text: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.

lessons.title: Do Not Be Hasty
lessons.hear:
“but those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint” (Isa 40:31).

This verse is often used to comfort the weary, but its point is that “waiting” is not draining but renewing. People who truly wait for God do not grow more tired the longer they wait; they grow stronger.

In relationships, the price of haste is often high: saying yes to anyone because you don’t want to be alone; compromising yourself to hold on to someone; rushing into a relationship to avoid being compared. These decisions often drain far more energy.

Xiaoxuan once stayed in an unsuitable relationship for two years because she was afraid of “running out of time.” Later she said: I thought waiting would make me lose out, but it was haste that made me lose the most.

We are not forced to stop; we are invited to be renewed in strength in God before taking the next step.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he often withdrew to lonely places to pray and was renewed in strength in God. The Bible is my standard: those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us calm and peace, so that we are not driven by anxiety. A person living selflessly finds safety not in “fast” but in “being in him.”
think: According to Isa 40:31, what do those who wait for the LORD receive?
In the past, what decision made out of haste drained me a great deal?
How can I face the pressure of relationships today in a calmer way?
lessons.speak: Lord, I often decide in a hurry because I am afraid of being alone and afraid of running out of time. Forgive my haste, and heal the fear in my heart. Renew my strength as I wait, so that I mount up with wings like eagles, and run and not be weary, walk and not faint. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, whenever you have a decision to make, first ask yourself: Am I acting out of peace, or out of fear? If out of fear, wait one more day and pray one more time.
lessons.quick: People who truly wait for God do not grow more tired the longer they wait; they grow stronger.
text: but those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.

lessons.title: A Season of Preparation
lessons.hear:
Luke sums up Jesus’ growth from age twelve to thirty in a single sentence: “Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men” (Luke 2:52).

His preparation had four dimensions: wisdom (mind), stature (body), favor with God (spirit), and favor with men (relationships). Thirty years of preparation led to three and a half years of ministry.

This gives us an important reminder: days of “waiting” can also be days of “preparation.” Preparation is not for obtaining a particular person, but for becoming a whole person.

You can ask yourself: In which area do I need to grow? In my mind, what do I need to learn? In my body, am I taking care of myself? In my spirit, how is my relationship with God? In my relationships, am I learning to be honest, to forgive, and to love?

A season of waiting is a lesson God has given us.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he used thirty years to prepare, growing in wisdom, stature, and favor with God and men. The Bible is my standard: preparation is growth in the whole of life. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he points out where we most need to grow. A person living selflessly does not use preparation to trade for a person, but submits to God’s shaping.
think: According to Luke 2:52, in which four areas did Jesus grow together?
Of these four areas, which one do I most need to grow in now?
This month, what concrete thing can I do in this area?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for letting Jesus show us what a life of preparation looks like. Lead me to grow in wisdom, body, spirit, and relationships, not to gain anything, but only to become a person who pleases you. Holy Spirit, point out where I most need to grow. Amen.
lessons.do: Make a chart of your “four areas”: mind, body, spirit, relationships. Write one small action for each area for this month, and post it where you will see it often.
lessons.quick: Days of waiting can also be days of preparation.
text: And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.

lessons.title: Commit Your Way to Him
lessons.hear:
Looking back over this week: trust in the LORD with all your heart and do not lean on your own understanding (Prov 3:5–6); God makes everything beautiful in its time (Eccl 3:11); those who wait will renew their strength (Isa 40:31); and Jesus used thirty years to prepare himself (Luke 2:52).

Finally, we read a verse that many people love to quote and that is easily misused: “Also delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart” (Ps 37:4).

This does not mean that if you are devout, God will give you the person you want. It means that when you delight in God, the desires of your heart will be changed and renewed. It goes on: “Commit your way to the LORD. Trust also in him, and he will do this” (Ps 37:5).

Committing is not giving up. It is taking your hands off the steering wheel and handing the direction to the best driver.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, entrusting everything to the Father; the Bible is my standard, for God’s timing is more accurate than our anxiety; the Holy Spirit is my guide, leading us as we wait. The order of relationships: first with God, then with myself, then with others. Let Jesus be King, and let the glory go to God.
think: This week, which sentence helped my anxiety the most?
According to Ps 37:4, what is different about the desires of the heart of one who delights in the LORD?
What is the one thing I most need to commit to God right now?
lessons.speak: LORD, I will delight in you. Renew the desires of my heart, so that I no longer compromise myself in my hurry to get something. I commit my way, my relationships, and my future to you; please bring it to pass. All the glory be to you. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal write: my biggest discovery this week; the one thing I will commit to God. Then say to a friend in one sentence: This week I am learning to commit one thing to God.
lessons.quick: Committing is not giving up; it is handing the direction to the best driver.
text: Also delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart.
Commit your way to the LORD. Trust also in him, and he will do this:

weeks.keyText: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.

weeks.title: Pride Is the Root of the Problem
weeks.theme: Control, silent treatment, and comparison in dating are all about leaving our place and grabbing power.
group: Read James 4:6. What is God’s attitude toward the proud, and toward the humble?
In an intimate relationship or a friendship, which expression of pride shows up most often for you (needing to win, the silent treatment, dredging up the past, comparing, controlling)?
This week, to whom are you willing to offer one honest apology or word of thanks? Ask your group to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, find a brother or sister whom you have hurt with your words, treated coldly, or compared yourself with, and say first: “What I said last time may have made you uncomfortable, and I want to say I’m sorry.” Do it not to get anything in return, but to let humility take the first step.
weeks.weekend: Pick a quiet time this weekend and write down the “pride” you have seen in yourself this week: where I want to win; where I want to control; where I compare. After you finish each item, say to God: Lord, I lay down power and return to my place. Then tear up the paper and write one sentence of thanks instead.

lessons.title: God Resists the Proud
lessons.hear:
Xiaoya and Zhe had been dating for six months when they argued over a small thing: who had failed to reply to a message first. Both felt they were not wrong, and neither would speak first. After three days of silent treatment, both were miserable, yet neither was willing to bow first.

James says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). This sentence points to the core problem in dating: many relationships fail not because of too little love, but because of unwillingness to bow the head.

3-2-1 defines pride very clearly: pride is leaving our place and grabbing power. It leaves the human place and grabs God’s authority, wanting to take God’s place. In dating, “I’m right,” “you should listen to me,” and “I won’t make this easy for you” are all ways of trying to sit in a seat that does not belong to us.

The good news is that the same verse also says God gives grace to the humble. We do not need to protect ourselves by winning, because God is already our protection.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: though he was God, he did not count equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself. The Bible is my standard: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he points out the pride in my heart and leads me back to my place. Pride is leaving our place and grabbing power; humility is laying down power and returning to our place, letting people be people and God be God.
think: According to James 4:6, how does God’s attitude differ toward the proud and the humble?
In a conflict in a relationship, what is hardest for me to let go of: face, reasons, or control?
In what matter can I lay down a little power first today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I admit that I often want to win, to control, and to make the other person bow first. Forgive my pride, so that I lay down the power that is not mine and return to the human place. Give me your grace, make me humble, and make me a peacemaker. Amen.
lessons.do: Whenever there is a moment today when you “want to win,” pause for ten seconds and say in your heart to God: I lay down this contest. Then choose to listen a little more and argue a little less.
lessons.quick: Many relationships fail not because of too little love, but because of unwillingness to bow the head.
text: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

lessons.title: Leaving Our Place
lessons.hear:
Where is the root of pride? Go back to the Garden of Eden. The serpent said to the woman: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Gen 3:5). The temptation in this sentence is not about what to eat, but about being “like God”: I define what is good and what is bad, and I decide what I want.

Humanity’s first fall was leaving our place and wanting to take God’s place. That root still lives in our hearts, and in every relationship.

Think about how often in dating we do the work of a “little god”: I decide where this relationship should go; I decide how the other person should respond to me; I decide who is right and who is wrong; I predict what the future will be; I make sure I won’t get hurt. None of these belongs to the human place.

The human place is to be loved, to trust, and to obey. God’s place is to govern, to define, and to protect. When each of us returns to our own place, there is peace in the heart.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: in the wilderness he was tempted to “act as God,” yet he chose to obey the Father. The Bible is my standard: the serpent’s temptation was to be “like God,” which is the root of all pride. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he leads us to see where we have played the little god. Self is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem; only selflessness lets God be God.
think: What is the temptation in Gen 3:5? What does “like God” mean?
In dating, which “little god” job do I most often do (controlling, predicting, defining right and wrong, protecting myself)?
How can I hand one of these back to God?
lessons.speak: Lord, I admit that I often want to be like God, deciding, controlling, and predicting everything. Forgive me for leaving my place, and bring me back to the human position: trusting you, obeying you, and being loved by you. Let me let God be God and let people be people. Amen.
lessons.do: Write this sentence in your journal: I decide, I control, I predict, I protect myself. Then next to each item write: Lord, I give it to you.
lessons.quick: The root of pride is wanting to be “like God”; the road to peace is returning to the human place.
text: for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

lessons.title: Pride in Dating
lessons.hear:
“Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” (Prov 16:18). The consequences of pride often show up first in relationships.

Pride in dating is not always loud. It may look like dredging up the past to prove you have always been right; the silent treatment, punishing the other person with silence; comparing, measuring your current partner against an ex or against other people’s partners; showing off, using your relationship status to prove your worth; or the resentment of “I’ve already given in so much,” quietly keeping score.

Pride may also wear the clothes of low self-esteem: “I can’t do anything right” or “I don’t deserve it,” which in fact puts all the attention on yourself.

In a conversation, Kai discovered that every time they argued, he would say, “You’re always like this!” Hidden in that sentence was a thought: I am the victim, and you are the offender. Later he learned to say, “I see that I’m responsible too.” Only then did the relationship begin to loosen.

Conviction is not agreeing with this principle; it is being willing to admit: I have it too.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: when he was reviled, he did not revile in return, and when falsely accused, he did not defend himself, but entrusted himself to the One who judges justly. The Bible is my standard: pride goes before destruction. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lets us see our pride, not to condemn us but to heal us. Humility overcomes pride, and humility leads to humility.
think: According to Prov 16:18, what follows pride and an arrogant spirit?
In dating or other relationships, which expression of pride appears most often in me?
If I am honest with myself, what part of the responsibility was mine in the most recent conflict?
lessons.speak: LORD, I admit that pride takes many forms, and some I have not even seen myself. Shine your light on me, so that I see the self and pride in my relationships. Forgive me, and give me the courage to say: I am responsible too. Amen.
lessons.do: Think back on the most recent conflict and write one sentence: What I am also responsible for is…. If you can, say this sentence to the other person today, without adding “but.”
lessons.quick: Conviction is being willing to admit: I have it too.
text: Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.

lessons.title: Control and Manipulation
lessons.hear:
When the disciples argued about who was the greatest, Jesus said that the kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called benefactors. Then he said: “the one who is greater among you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves” (Luke 22:26).

Jesus reversed the direction of power: in his Kingdom, being great is not about managing people but about serving them.

This is an important reminder for dating. Control is not always violence; it is often packaged as “concern”: requiring daily check-ins on where you are, checking the other person’s phone, using “If you loved me, you would…” as blackmail, using coldness or tears to force the other to give in, and isolating the other from friends.

All of these behaviors are grabbing power. Love is not keeping the other person under my control, but giving the other person to God and being willing to sacrifice for his or her good.

If you are the one being controlled: you are not failing to love enough, and it is not your fault. Please tell someone you trust; if there are threats, violence, or fear, please seek help first (see “I Need Help” in the app).
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he washed his disciples’ feet and used power to serve. The Bible is my standard: the one who is greater should be like the one who serves. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he points out the ways we control people and gives us the power to let go. Selfless love does not hold people in its hand but places them in God’s hand.
think: In Luke 22:26, how does Jesus redefine being “great”?
In a relationship, have I tried to control the other person through concern, emotions, or conditions?
If I am the one being controlled, which trusted person can I turn to for help?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for showing what serving love is. Forgive me for trying to control people in many ways; make me willing to let go and place those I love in your hands. If anyone is being controlled right now, protect them, give them wisdom and courage, and let them receive help. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, do not check anyone’s phone, posts, or whereabouts. If you find you badly want to look, first pray to God, and tell a companion about the urge.
lessons.quick: Love is not holding people in your hand, but placing them in God’s hand.
text: He said to them, “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’
But not so with you. Rather, the one who is greater among you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves.

lessons.title: Humbly Returning to Our Place
lessons.hear:
Looking back over this week: God resists the proud (James 4:6); the root of pride is wanting to be like God (Gen 3:5); pride takes many forms in dating (Prov 16:18); and Jesus reversed power into service (Luke 22:26).

Peter gives us the way out: “clothe yourselves with humility and subject yourselves to one another” (1 Pet 5:5), and then: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God” (1 Pet 5:6).

In the original language, “clothe yourselves” carries the sense of putting on or tying on, like a servant tying on an apron to get ready to serve. Humility is not weakness and not thinking little of yourself, but being willing to lay down power and return to your place.

3-2-1 says: humility overcomes pride. Pride provokes pride, and both lose; humility leads to humility, and both win. Today, you can be the one who is humble first.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, laying down power to serve people; the Bible is my standard, for God gives grace to the humble; the Holy Spirit is my guide, helping us see our pride and return to our place. The order of relationships: first with God, then with myself, then with others. Let Jesus be King, and let the glory go to God.
think: This week, what is the greatest pride I have seen in myself?
In 1 Pet 5:6, under whose hand are we to humble ourselves? How does that relate to “laying down power”?
To whom can I say one humble word first today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, teach me humility, so that I lay down power and return to the place you have set for me. Make me the one who is humble first, leading others to humility too, so that our relationships have your grace. All the glory be to you. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal write: my biggest discovery this week; the one person I will be humble toward first. Then say one sentence to this person today: Thank you, or: I’m sorry.
lessons.quick: Humility leads to humility; today, you can take the first step.
text: Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility and subject yourselves to one another; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time,

weeks.keyText: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

weeks.title: Don’t Make Your Partner Your Savior
weeks.theme: Treating romance as the source of happiness means looking in a person for what only God can give.
group: Read Exod 20:3 and Ezek 14:3. An idol is not always a stone statue; what else might it be?
If one text message or one reaction from the other person can decide your mood for the whole day, what expectation do you think lies behind it?
This week, which need that “only God can meet” are you willing to take back from other people and hand over to God? Ask your group members to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: At Sunday worship, choose your favorite song and sing it wholeheartedly to God: “You are my satisfaction.” After the service, don’t check your phone right away. First share with a brother or sister: this week, in what situation did I place my expectations on a person?
weeks.weekend: This weekend, set aside a half day to “fast from people’s expectations”: don’t send messages looking for comfort, don’t scroll social media to see who reacted, and don’t measure yourself by anyone else’s response. Spend the time in devotion, exercise, and serving. Afterward, write down: I discovered that what I most often ask people for is…

lessons.title: You Shall Have No Other Gods
lessons.hear:
The first of the Ten Commandments is: “You shall have no other gods before me.” (Exod 20:3) Many people think this commandment simply means we shouldn’t worship idols made of stone. But in the Bible, the meaning of an idol goes deeper: anything that takes the place of God is an idol.

Idols are often not bad things but good things: family, career, money, achievement, and of course, romantic love. Love itself is God’s design, but when we say, “I can’t live without him,” or, “I only have worth if I have him,” love has been put in God’s place.

This doesn’t mean we may not love someone deeply. It means that loving a person must come under God. In its right place, love is a gift; in God’s place, love becomes a burden, and the other person cannot bear it either.

God is a jealous God, not because he is petty, but because he knows that only he can carry our lives.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he put the Father first, and even the people dearest to him came after that order. The Bible is my standard: besides God, there shall be no other gods. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he shows me what has taken hold of my heart. The order of relationships: first God, then self, then others, then things. When the order is reversed, love becomes distorted.
think: What does Exod 20:3 say we must not have?
If I listed “the three most important things” in my life, where would God rank?
What can I do today to put God back in first place?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that I often put good things in your place, including romance and other people’s approval. Forgive me, and help me put you first. Help me love people without treating them as God, and without handing myself over to anything that cannot carry me. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, make a small “declaration of order”: in the morning, as soon as you open your eyes, say to God, “Lord, you are first.” Only then pick up your phone.
lessons.quick: Love under God is a gift; love in God’s place becomes a burden.
text: “You shall have no other gods before me.

lessons.title: Idols in the Heart
lessons.hear:
The book of Ezekiel has a startling line: “these men have taken their idols into their heart.” (Ezek 14:3) Idols aren’t placed in temples; they are placed in the heart.

Idols in the heart are hard to see. A few questions can help you check: Is there someone whose one message can decide my mood for the day? Have I compromised my values or my faith to keep a relationship going? Has my life lost its meaning because someone left? Do I often think, “If I just had him, all my problems would be solved”?

Xiaoxin realized that the first thing she did every day was check whether he had replied. When he didn’t, she was restless all day, and she didn’t even have the strength to pray. In tears she said to God, “I think I’ve put him above you.” That day, her real healing began.

Seeing is not for condemnation, but for freedom.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he said that whoever loves father or mother more than him is not worthy to be his disciple. The Bible is my standard: idols can live in the heart. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he shines his light on us and reveals hidden idols. A person living for self puts people in God’s place; a person living in selflessness puts God back in God’s place.
think: According to Ezek 14:3, where had they taken their idols?
Which person or thing most affects my mood and decisions right now?
How can I give that place back to God?
lessons.speak: Lord, shine your light on the idols in my heart, and show me whom and what I have put in your place. I don’t need to hide; I am willing to be honest. Forgive me and cleanse me, so that my heart turns completely to you and worships you alone. Amen.
lessons.do: Write in your journal: There is a person whose response affects my mood the most. That person is… Then say to God: “I give this place back to you.”
lessons.quick: Idols can live in the heart; seeing them is for the sake of freedom.
text: “Son of man, these men have taken their idols into their heart, and put the stumbling block of their iniquity before their face. Should I be inquired of at all by them?

lessons.title: Broken Cisterns
lessons.hear:
Jeremiah speaks for God: “they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut out cisterns for themselves: broken cisterns that can’t hold water.” (Jer 2:13) God says his people committed two evils: first, they forsook the spring of living water; second, they dug cisterns for themselves, and broken ones at that.

This picture is especially meaningful for matters of the heart. Everyone has a thirst inside: to be loved, accepted, and valued. God originally placed this thirst in us to draw us toward him. But too often we don’t go to the spring; we dig our own cisterns instead, trying to fill this thirst with a relationship, a person’s approval, or an ambiguous romance.

The problem is that the cisterns are broken. It’s not that the other person is bad; it’s that a person simply can’t hold that much. When we press all our needs onto one person, they grow weary, and we end up disappointed.

Conviction means admitting: I need the spring, not just a cistern.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his food was to do the will of the one who sent him. The Bible is my standard: forsaking the spring of living water is an evil. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he brings us back to the spring. A person living for self uses others to prove their worth; a person living in selflessness is already loved and no longer lives on other people’s responses.
think: According to Jer 2:13, what two evils did God’s people commit?
What do I most often use to fill the thirst in my heart (relationships, praise, ambiguous romance, work, entertainment)?
If I brought this thirst to God, what would I say to him?
lessons.speak: God, you are the spring of living water. I confess that I often leave you to dig my own cisterns, using people and things to fill the thirst in my heart. Forgive me, and bring me back to you, so that I may find satisfaction in you, and the ability to love others. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, when you want to open your phone to look for comfort, a reply, or a compliment, stop first and spend three minutes telling God about your thirst. Then decide whether to open it.
lessons.quick: When we press all our needs onto one person, they grow weary, and we end up disappointed.
text: “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut out cisterns for themselves: broken cisterns that can’t hold water.

lessons.title: The Spring of Living Water
lessons.hear:
Jesus met a Samaritan woman at a well. She came alone at noon to draw water, because she didn’t want to run into anyone. Jesus saw her thirst and said, “whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again.” (John 4:14)

This woman had been through several relationships. Again and again she used a relationship to quench her thirst, and again and again she was thirsty. Jesus didn’t shame her; he gently pointed out that her thirst needed a different kind of water.

He said that the water he gives will become in a person a well springing up to eternal life. That means we no longer look for water only from the outside, but receive a never-ending flow of life from within.

This is the key to our dating life: we don’t first look for someone to satisfy us; we first receive life from Jesus, and then we have the power to give to others. A person who is satisfied in God no longer takes from people, but pours out to them.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he doesn’t shame people; he leads them to see their real thirst. The Bible is my standard: the water Jesus gives means a person never thirsts again. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he is the living water flowing within us. Selflessness is not having nothing, but entering the limitless: from the fullness of Jesus, we receive grace upon grace.
think: What does Jesus promise in John 4:14?
What is the deepest thirst in my heart? How have I tried to quench it in the past?
How can I receive from Jesus today, instead of begging from people?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for not shaming me, but gently pointing out my thirst. Give me the living water, so that I become a spring within, no longer begging people for love, but receiving from you and then pouring out to others. Holy Spirit, flow within me. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, read John 4:1–26, then choose one sentence and write it down: What Jesus is saying to me is… Make this sentence your prayer for today.
lessons.quick: A person who is satisfied in God no longer takes from people, but pours out to them.
text: Jesus answered her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again,
but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.”

lessons.title: Only You Can Satisfy Me
lessons.hear:
Looking back over this week: no other gods (Exod 20:3); idols can live in the heart (Ezek 14:3); forsaking the spring of living water leaves us with broken cisterns (Jer 2:13); Jesus gives living water so that a person never thirsts again (John 4:14).

David’s psalm gives us a positive way out: “In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more.” (Ps 16:11) Satisfaction is not found anywhere else; it is found in God’s presence.

This doesn’t deny human love; it finds a place for it. When we are first satisfied in God’s presence, our love for others is no longer taking but a gift; our sense of our own worth no longer depends on others but comes from God; and our hope for the future is no longer tied to a certain person but to him.

This week, which cistern was shown to be broken? Don’t be discouraged; this is exactly where the way back to the spring begins.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example; he was satisfied in the Father’s presence. The Bible is my standard; only God can satisfy us. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he brings us back to the spring. The order of relationships: first God, then self, then others. Let Jesus be King, and let all the glory go to God.
think: This week, which broken cistern did I see myself digging?
According to Ps 16:11, where is fullness of joy?
Which need can I take back from people right now and hand over to God?
lessons.speak: Lord, in your presence is fullness of joy, and in your right hand there are pleasures forever more. Correct the idols in my heart, so that I no longer ask people for what only you can give. I give you my thirst and my hope. All glory be to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Write in your journal: my biggest discovery this week; one expectation I will take back from another person. Then pray for one minute for the person on whom you have placed those expectations.
lessons.quick: When we are first satisfied in God’s presence, love for others is no longer taking, but a gift.
text: You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more.
