weeks.title: Selfless Love
weeks.theme: No longer I, but Christ: selflessness is not having nothing, but entering the limitless.
group: Read Gal 2:20. When Paul says “no longer I,” what does he mean? How is that different from losing yourself?
What misunderstandings have you had about “selflessness” and “denying yourself”? Which misunderstanding was corrected this week?
In which relationship do you want to practice responding with “Christ lives in me” this week? Ask your group members to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After Sunday worship, find a partner and share with each other: this week, at what moment did I choose to let Christ lead rather than my emotions? Pray for each other’s next practice. When you get home, write today’s one sentence in the notes app on your phone.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, pick one setting where you’ll be with people (a family meal, a gathering with friends, or serving) and pray beforehand: Lord, let it be Christ living in me today. During the gathering, deliberately ask one more question, listen to one more sentence, and defend yourself less. Afterward, write in your journal: I saw…

lessons.title: No Longer I
lessons.hear:
After Lin heard the word “selflessness,” she decided to “stop thinking of herself altogether.” So in her relationship, she gave in on everything: when he was late, she said it was fine; when he said hurtful things, she said it was fine; when he asked her to give up Sunday worship, she said that was fine too. Six months later, she felt that she had disappeared.

This is not selflessness; this is losing yourself. Paul means something different. He says, “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Gal 2:20) It is no longer “I” on the throne but Christ; I have not vanished, but Christ has taken over the leading role in my life.

Selflessness is not having nothing, but entering the limitless. It is neither low self-worth nor people-pleasing; it is letting Christ’s love, Christ’s wisdom, and Christ’s courage live out through me. Because a truly selfless person is filled with Christ, they dare to speak the truth, and they dare to say no.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he obeyed the Father completely, yet never lost himself; he dared to say no, and he dared to say yes. The Bible is my standard: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lets Christ’s life be lived out in me. Only through selflessness can I let Jesus be King and be led by the Holy Spirit.
think: According to Gal 2:20, who is the one who lives now?
Have I misunderstood “selflessness” as losing myself or always giving in?
In what situation today can I let Christ live in me, instead of relying on my own reaction?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for loving me and giving yourself up for me. Correct my misunderstanding of selflessness, so that I don’t lose myself but let you live in me. Holy Spirit, give me your love in my relationships, along with your wisdom and courage. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, when you feel like losing your temper, turning cold, or pleasing people too much, pause for ten seconds and say in your heart: Lord, not me, but you in me. Then choose a response that pleases God.
lessons.quick: Selflessness is not losing yourself, but letting Christ live in me.
text: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.

lessons.title: Denying Yourself
lessons.hear:
Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23) Notice two details: first, it is a daily matter, so denying yourself is not a one-time decision but a choice made every day; second, it is “his” cross, because everyone’s cross is different.

In the 3-2-1 ideology, denying yourself means: for Jesus, for others, not for yourself. It doesn’t deny your own worth; it simply no longer lets yourself be the center of your life.

In dating, denying yourself is often very concrete: when you want to prove you’re right, choosing to listen; when you want to be noticed, choosing to care for the other person; when you want to hold on, choosing to let go; when you want to indulge, choosing self-control.

We deny ourselves not to get something, but because we have come to know Jesus and have seen him give himself up for us, and we are willing to love with that same heart.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he gave himself up for us and laid down his life. The Bible is my standard: take up the cross daily and follow the Lord. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us power to choose self-denial every day. A person living for self asks, “What can I get?” A person living in selflessness asks, “What can I do for Jesus and for others?”
think: What three things does Luke 9:23 say a follower of Jesus must do?
What is the one thing I’m clinging to that I most need to “let go of” today?
What small thing can I do for my partner or a friend without expecting anything in return?
lessons.speak: Lord, I want to follow you, but I often can’t bear to let go of myself. Give me strength to choose self-denial every day, for you and for others, not just for myself. Teach me to set myself down in small things, and to be faithful and obedient to you in big things. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, do one small thing “for others, not for yourself”: pour someone a glass of water, give up your seat, or thank someone first. Don’t let anyone see it, and don’t expect a response.
lessons.quick: Denying yourself is for Jesus and for others, not for yourself.
text: He said to all, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.

lessons.title: The Mind of Christ
lessons.hear:
Paul wrote to the church in Philippi, where there was rivalry and conflict. He said, “in humility, each counting others better than himself.” (Phil 2:3) Then he told them, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Phil 2:5)

What kind of mind did Christ Jesus have? The verses that follow say that he was in the form of God, yet did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross.

This is an example no one can match. He had power, yet chose to lay it down; he deserved honor, yet chose to serve.

In dating, “counting others better than yourself” is not low self-worth. It is seeing the other person’s goodness and respecting their worth, without putting them down to lift yourself up. When both people look at each other with the mind of Christ, the relationship changes from competition to helping each other flourish.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he had power, yet chose to lay it down; he deserved honor, yet chose to serve. The Bible is my standard: have in your mind what was also in Christ Jesus. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he shapes in us the heart of Christ. A selfless person in a relationship doesn’t compare or compete, but helps the other flourish.
think: With what attitude does Phil 2:3–5 tell us to look at others?
In my relationship, have I unknowingly been comparing myself with the other person or competing with them?
What is one strength of the other person that I can appreciate specifically today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you had power, yet you chose to serve; you deserved honor, yet you chose humility. Put your mind in me, so that I no longer compare myself with others but see the goodness in them. Make me someone who helps others flourish. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, tell someone you value one specific thing you appreciate about them, without adding any “but,” and without expecting a response.
lessons.quick: Have the mind of Christ: not competing, but helping each other flourish.
text: doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,

lessons.title: Submitting to One Another
lessons.hear:
Paul says, “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.” (Eph 5:21) This sentence is often brought up when talking about marriage, but it is first spoken to all believers.

Notice three key phrases. The first is “one another”: it is not one person submitting to the other in one direction, but both submitting to each other. The second is “in the fear of Christ”: the one we ultimately submit to is Christ, not the other person’s temper or demands. The third is “subjecting yourselves”: it is voluntary and comes from love; it is not forced.

In dating, practicing “submitting to one another” includes: talking over important decisions together instead of announcing them one-sidedly; when you disagree, each praying and being willing to hear the other’s reasons; and being willing to accept it when the other person points out my weakness.

It must be emphasized: submitting to one another is not obeying control. If one person demands unconditional compliance from the other, even pressuring them with threats or humiliation, that is not the fear of Christ but an abuse of power.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he submitted to the Father, and he respected every person’s freedom. The Bible is my standard: submitting to one another comes from the fear of Christ. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us power to submit and respect willingly. A selfless person is willing to be examined and, in love, to help the other flourish, without using power.
think: According to Eph 5:21, what is the reason for submitting, and to whom is it owed?
In my relationship, do I often want to be submitted to, or am I willing to submit?
What is the difference between “submitting to one another” and “obeying control”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I revere you, and I am willing to submit to others in your love. Make me willing to listen and to be examined, and keep me from using power to pressure others. If anyone is being controlled right now, give them wisdom and courage, and help them find help. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, on one decision that involves another person, first ask them, “What do you think?” Listen carefully until they finish, and then share your own thoughts.
lessons.quick: Submitting to one another is voluntary, out of fear of Christ, and is not obeying control.
text: subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.

lessons.title: Selflessness Brings Unity
lessons.hear:
Looking back over this week: no longer I, but Christ (Gal 2:20); deny yourself daily and follow Jesus (Luke 9:23); have the mind of Christ (Phil 2:3–5); submit to one another (Eph 5:21).

In his prayer before he was arrested, Jesus pointed all of this toward one goal: “that they may be one, even as we are one.” (John 17:22) And he said, “I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one.” (John 17:23)

Unity is not two people squeezed into one, nor one person swallowing up the other, but two people both in Christ, filled by the same Christ.

Two people living for self wear each other out; only two selfless people can truly be one. So preparing for dating is not first finding that person, but first becoming a person filled with Christ.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example; he is one with the Father, and one with us. The Bible is my standard; only selflessness can bring unity. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he lives Christ out in us. The order of relationships: first God, then self, then others. Let Jesus be King, and let all the glory go to God.
think: This week, which sentence gave me a new insight into “selflessness”?
According to John 17:22–23, what is the basis of unity?
In which relationship do I most need selflessness right now?
lessons.speak: Father God, thank you for making Jesus one with you, and for making us one in Christ. Correct me, so that I no longer love people by the strength of self but let Christ live in me. Make me a person who can be one with others. All glory be to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Write in your journal: my biggest discovery this week; one place where I need selflessness. Then pray: Lord, let Christ live here.
lessons.quick: Only two selfless people can truly be one.
text: The glory which you have given me, I have given to them, that they may be one, even as we are one,
I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one, that the world may know that you sent me and loved them, even as you loved me.

weeks.title: The Order of Relationships
weeks.theme: God first, then self, then others, then things; when the order is right, love stands firm.
group: Read Matt 22:37–39. Which commandment does Jesus put first? What is the second?
In your life right now, what is the actual order of God, self, others, and things? Which one most needs adjusting?
This week, which relationship do you want to repair first, or which thing do you want to put back in its proper order? Ask your group members to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After Sunday worship, find a brother or sister and spend two minutes telling each other, “The order of my life right now is…” Then spend three minutes praying together over that order. When you get home, write “God, self, others, things” on a sticky note and put it where you will see it often.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, set aside a half day for an “order check”: in the first hour, be alone with God; in the second hour, take care of yourself (exercise, rest, tidying up); in the third hour, reach out to one person (arrange to meet or give them a call); only then deal with tasks. Afterward, write down: When the order is right, what is different in my heart?

lessons.title: Love the Lord with All Your Heart
lessons.hear:
Someone asked Jesus which commandment in the law is the greatest. Jesus answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.” (Matt 22:37) Then he said that this is the first and great commandment (Matt 22:38).

Notice that Jesus says “all”: all your heart, all your soul, all your mind, meaning your whole person. Loving God is not one part of life; it is the first thing in life, and its root.

This order matters especially for dating. Many people’s relationships are like a ladder leaned against the wrong wall: the higher you climb, the more dangerous it gets. For his girlfriend’s sake, Xiaofeng skipped his small group and his service for half a year. He said, “I love her, so I’m willing to give up everything for her.” The result was that the relationship grew heavier and heavier, because she had become his everything, and that became her burden.

Putting God first doesn’t weaken your ability to love people; it gives your love roots, strength, and boundaries.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his first was always the Father. The Bible is my standard: to love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and mind is the first and great commandment. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he kindles in us a fire to love God. The order of relationships: first build a relationship with God. When the order is right, everything else can stand firm.
think: According to Matt 22:37, to what degree are we to love God?
Has my relationship with God been pushed to the back by another relationship?
What can I do today to set aside a block of time just for God?
lessons.speak: Lord, I want to love you with all my heart, all my soul, and all my mind. Forgive me for putting other things before you, and help me come to you first, receive love from you, and then go love others. Make you the first in my life and my root. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, put your devotions before your phone: spend ten minutes alone with God first, and only then reply to any messages. If you’ve already missed it, make it up before bed.
lessons.quick: Putting God first gives love roots, strength, and boundaries.
text: Jesus said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’
This is the first and great commandment.

lessons.title: Love Your Neighbor as Yourself
lessons.hear:
Jesus went on to say, “A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” (Matt 22:39) This sentence is often simplified to “you have to love yourself first before you can love others,” but that isn’t really Jesus’ point.

What Jesus is saying is: treat others the way you treat yourself. You know you get hungry, so you know others get hungry too; you know you’re afraid of being rejected, so you know others are too; you want to be respected, so respect others as well.

It also implies that we should have a healthy relationship with ourselves. That relationship is neither self-obsession nor self-blame, but this: accepting the person God made, being honest about my weaknesses, and taking care of my body and mind.

Someone who is long accustomed to self-blame, people-pleasing, and suppressing themselves will find it hard to love others in a healthy way, because there is no peace in their heart. So the order is: first God, then reconciling with yourself, then walking with others.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he knew who he was, and he respected every person. The Bible is my standard: love your neighbor as yourself, treating others the way I want to be treated. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he heals my relationship with myself so that I can accept, be honest with, and take care of myself. Selflessness is not thinking little of yourself, but no longer making yourself the center.
think: According to Matt 22:39, how are we to love others?
Is my relationship with myself more like self-blame, people-pleasing, or acceptance?
How can I be a little kinder to myself today, and a little kinder to others too?
lessons.speak: God, thank you for making me; I am loved by you. Heal my relationship with myself, so that I don’t blame myself or try to please everyone, but am honest, accepting, and caring toward myself. Help me love others the way you love me. And teach me to see your image in others too. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, do one good thing for yourself: eat a good meal, go to bed earlier, or write down three things you’re thankful for. Then do one good thing for someone else, with the same heart.
lessons.quick: Treat others the way you want to be treated.

lessons.title: Seek First His Kingdom
lessons.hear:
“But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matt 6:33) The background of this verse is Jesus talking about worry: what to eat, what to wear. He says that your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things, so seek first his Kingdom and his righteousness.

The word “first” matters here for the sake of order. It doesn’t say that everything else is unimportant; it says that the order must not be reversed.

This verse is often misread as a kind of deal: if I seek God first, God will give me the person I want. That is not what it means. What it means is that when we put God’s Kingdom first, God takes care of our other needs, and our view of those needs is changed as well.

Relationships are also a need God cares about. We don’t have to be anxious about it, but we can place it in God’s hands and first focus on the work of his Kingdom.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he sought the Father’s Kingdom and righteousness first, and the Father took care of all his other needs. The Bible is my standard: seek first his Kingdom and his righteousness. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he brings our priorities in line with God’s heart. A selfless person doesn’t treat God as a tool for getting what they want, but is satisfied in God himself.
think: According to Matt 6:33, what are we to seek first?
Have I treated “seeking God first” as a way to get a certain result?
What work of “God’s Kingdom” can I do first today?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for knowing everything I need. Help me seek your Kingdom and your righteousness first, and not treat you as a tool for getting my wishes. Take care of my needs, and renew what I ask for, so that my heart turns single-mindedly to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, spend ten minutes praying for a church, a missionary, or someone in need, and only then pray for your own needs.
lessons.quick: The order must not be reversed: seek God’s Kingdom first, and everything else is in his hands.
text: But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.

lessons.title: People Matter More Than Things
lessons.hear:
Martha welcomed Jesus into her home, and she was busy preparing many things. But Mary sat at Jesus’ feet, listening to his teaching. Martha was upset and asked Jesus to tell Mary to come help. Jesus answered, “but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.” (Luke 10:42)

What Martha was doing wasn’t bad; she was serving. But she put “things” before “people,” including Jesus himself.

The 3-2-1 ideology has a very practical saying: people matter more than things, and relationships matter more than possessions. Don’t hurt people for the sake of things, and don’t damage a relationship for the sake of possessions.

This is very common in both dating and ministry: busy with meetings, rushing projects, and doing service, yet with no time to truly listen to the people beside us; or, for the sake of making money and achieving things, neglecting relationships.

When we put people before things, we are following Jesus’ example: he always stopped for people.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he stopped for people and saw them one by one. The Bible is my standard: only one thing is needed, and that is to be in the Lord’s presence. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he reminds us that people matter more than things. A selfless person isn’t driven by tasks, but lets relationships come before work.
think: In Luke 10:42, which one thing does Jesus say is needed?
Am I neglecting someone important (including God) right now because I’m busy?
For whom can I put aside one task today and spend time with them?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I am often like Martha, busy with many things and neglecting you and the people around me. Forgive me, and make me willing to stop for people. Help me, even in my busyness, to still choose the good part. And remind me that every encounter is something you have entrusted to me. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose someone important (family, a friend, or a companion), put down what you’re doing, and talk with them for ten minutes. Don’t look at your phone, don’t give advice, just listen.
lessons.quick: People matter more than things; stopping for people is following Jesus’ example.
text: Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.title: Be Reconciled to Your Brother
lessons.hear:
Looking back over this week: love God first (Matt 22:37–38); love your neighbor as yourself (Matt 22:39); seek God’s Kingdom first (Matt 6:33); people matter more than things (Luke 10:42).

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says something weighty: “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” (Matt 5:24) He puts reconciliation with people before worship.

This doesn’t mean people matter more than God. It means that our relationship with God shows itself in our relationships with people. If a relationship is broken and we leave it unaddressed, our closeness with God will be affected too.

This week, you may have seen some part of the order out of place: God pushed to the back, yourself neglected, others left out in the cold, or tasks taking over your life. Don’t be discouraged; the order can be adjusted, starting today.

With this, the eight weeks of the conceptual stage are complete. Next, we move into life itself and see what love truly looks like.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example; he held loving God and loving people together. The Bible is my standard; loving God is first, and loving others is second. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he helps us adjust the order. The order of relationships: first God, then self, then others, then things. Let Jesus be King, and let all the glory go to God.
think: This week, which part of the order did I see most needs adjusting?
According to Matt 5:24, what must be done before offering the gift?
Is there a relationship that needs reconciliation right now? What is the first step?
lessons.speak: Father, help me put the order right: love you first, then be reconciled with myself, then walk with others, and then handle my tasks. Give me courage to take the initiative to repair the relationships that need repairing. All glory be to you. And hold me up where I have fallen, so that I can stand again. Amen.
lessons.do: Write in your journal: my biggest discovery this week; one order I will adjust; one person I want to reconcile with. Then today, take the first step toward that person: send a message, or arrange to meet.
lessons.quick: The order can be adjusted, starting today.
text: “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
